source: Zellem et al. (2014), ApJ 790, 53, 'The 4.5 um full-orbit phase curve of the hot Jupiter HD 209458b' (doi:10.1088/0004-637X/790/1/53; arXiv:1405.5923). Spitzer IRAC 4.5 um, program 60021, 2010 January 17 to 21. Values read from the authors' LaTeX source: the phase-curve equation in section 2.3, Table 2 (Global Fit Parameters) and Table 3 (Brightness Temperatures).

eclipseDepth.where: Table 2, Second Secondary Eclipse Depth. Section 2.3: 'we use the deeper measured secondary eclipse depth to establish this baseline'.

model.equation: F = 1 + c0 + c1 cos(2 pi t/P) + c2 sin(2 pi t/P) + c3 cos(4 pi t/P) + c4 sin(4 pi t/P) (section 2.3), with c3 and c4 dropped because the BIC showed they do not improve the fit. The planet's flux is F - 1. The paper does not print c0; the planet's flux at mid-eclipse is taken to be the deeper eclipse depth, which the paper names as the baseline.

daysideK.where: Table 3, Second Secondary Eclipse (the depth this record uses)

offsetDegrees.cell: -40.9 +/- 6.0 degrees; 9.6 +/- 1.4 hours before secondary eclipse, a hot spot 40.9 +/- 6.0 degrees east

notStated: Where t = 0 falls. Only t counted from mid-transit puts the curve's peak 40.9 degrees before eclipse and its trough 40.9 degrees before transit, as Table 2 gives them; the test checks both.
The stellar brightness temperature behind Table 3. The one the second eclipse's depth and 1443 K imply, 5588 K at 4.5 um, turns the curve's maximum and minimum into 1497 K and 972 K.
